nodes.label: Electromagnetic Induction
nodes.note: Induced EMF arises whenever magnetic flux changes, through motion, changing fields, or changing current. JEE Main tests Lenz's sign rule, motional EMF, self-inductance, and $R$-$L$ transients. Use $$\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$ as the starting point.

nodes.label: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.group: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.note: Flux through a loop and the two Faraday laws set the induced EMF magnitude. Lenz's law fixes its opposing direction. Flux linkage is $$N\Phi_B = NBA\cos\theta$$.

nodes.label: Magnetic Flux
nodes.group: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.note: The flux through an area $A$ in field $B$ is $$\Phi_B = \int \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta$$ where $\theta$ is between $\vec{B}$ and the area normal. Its SI unit is the weber.

nodes.label: Faraday's Laws
nodes.group: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.note: Induced EMF equals the rate of change of flux linkage: $$\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$. The negative sign encodes Lenz's law; magnitude grows with turns $N$.

nodes.label: Lenz's Law and Energy
nodes.group: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.note: The induced current opposes the change in flux that produces it. This is energy conservation: external work done against the opposition equals electrical energy dissipated. Energy balance reads $$F_{ext}v = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{R}$$.

nodes.label: Average and Instantaneous EMF
nodes.group: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.note: Average EMF over an interval is $$\varepsilon_{avg} = -N\frac{\Delta \Phi_B}{\Delta t}$$ while the instantaneous value is the derivative. Quick rotation or fast field change gives large peaks.

nodes.label: Motional EMF
nodes.note: A conductor moving through a magnetic field separates charges and creates motional EMF along its length. Hall balance gives $$E = vB$$ inside the moving conductor.

nodes.label: Translational Motional EMF
nodes.note: A rod of length $l$ moving at speed $v$ perpendicular to $B$ develops $$\varepsilon = Blv$$ along its length. Force balance $qvB = qE$ gives the steady field $E = vB$.

nodes.label: Rotational Motional EMF
nodes.note: A rod rotating at angular speed $\omega$ about one end in a field $B$ gives $$\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$$ from integrating $v = \omega r$. A disc between rim and center gives $\frac{1}{2}B\omega R^2$.

nodes.label: Motional EMF as Flux Rule
nodes.note: Sweeping area changes linked flux: $\varepsilon = Blv$ equals $d\Phi/dt$ with $\Phi = BA$. The flux rule unifies translational and rotational cases. Flux through the swept area is $$\Phi_B = Blx$$, so $$\varepsilon = Blv$$.

nodes.label: Non-Conservative Induced Electric Fields
nodes.note: A changing magnetic field creates a circulating, non-conservative electric field even with no conductor present. Maxwell-Faraday: $$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$.

nodes.label: Maxwell-Faraday Equation
nodes.note: In differential form $$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$ shows the induced field circulates. It has no scalar potential and nonzero curl.

nodes.label: Cylindrical Region of Changing B
nodes.note: Inside a uniform region of radius $R$ with changing $B$, symmetry gives $$E_\phi \cdot 2\pi r = -\pi r^2 \frac{dB}{dt} \Rightarrow E_\phi = -\frac{r}{2}\frac{dB}{dt}$$ for $r < R$.

nodes.label: Electron in Induced Field
nodes.note: A charge $q$ free to move in the induced field feels $F = qE_\phi$ and a tangential acceleration. Energy comes from the changing magnetic flux, not from a battery. A free charge accelerates with $$a = \frac{qE_\phi}{m}$$.

nodes.label: Conducting Rod on Rails
nodes.note: A sliding rod on rails forms a circuit whose motion generates current, force, and feedback; capacitor or constant-force variants test dynamics. Drag force is $$F = \frac{B^2l^2v}{R}$$.

nodes.label: Rod with Resistor
nodes.note: A rod on rails closed through $R$ carries $$I = \frac{Blv}{R}$$ and feels drag $F = BIl = \frac{B^2 l^2 v}{R}$. Terminal speed under constant force is $v_t = FR/(B^2 l^2)$.

nodes.label: Rod Across a Capacitor
nodes.note: With a capacitor $C$ and no resistor, EMF charges it: $$Blv = \frac{Q}{C} \Rightarrow Q = CBlv$$. Differentiating gives $I = CBl\,a$, so a constant force yields constant acceleration $a = F/(m + B^2C l^2)$.

nodes.label: Terminal Velocity Feedback
nodes.note: Drag rises linearly with speed, so current decays as the rod approaches steady speed. Force balance $F_{ext} = \frac{B^2 l^2 v}{R}$ yields terminal velocity. Use $$\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$ as the starting point.

nodes.label: Inductance: Self and Mutual
nodes.note: Self and mutual inductance quantify how a circuit's own or a neighbor's current links flux to it. For a solenoid, $$L = \mu_0 n^2 V$$.

nodes.label: Self-Inductance
nodes.note: Self-inductance is flux linkage per unit current: $$L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I}$$ and induced EMF is $\varepsilon = -L\,dI/dt$. For a long solenoid $L = \mu_0 n^2 V$.

nodes.label: Mutual Inductance
nodes.note: Flux linkage in coil 2 due to current in coil 1 defines $$M = \frac{N_2\Phi_{21}}{I_1}$$ with EMF $\varepsilon_2 = -M\,dI_1/dt$. Reciprocity gives $M_{12} = M_{21}$.

nodes.label: Energy Stored in Inductor
nodes.note: Work building current in an inductor is stored as magnetic energy $$U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\times \text{volume}$$ This energy lives in the magnetic field itself.

nodes.label: Coupling Coefficient
nodes.note: Coupling $k$ measures shared flux: $$M = k\sqrt{L_1 L_2}, \ 0 \le k \le 1$$. JEE asks turns ratio effects and whether coils aid or oppose.

nodes.label: RL and LC Transients
nodes.note: Switching an inductor or capacitor into a resistor creates exponential growth or decay of current and charge. Time constant $$\tau = L/R$$ sets the transient scale.

nodes.label: RL Current Growth
nodes.note: Closing the switch gives $$I(t) = \frac{V}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \quad \tau = \frac{L}{R}$$. Current starts at zero and saturates at $V/R$.

nodes.label: RL Current Decay
nodes.note: Shorting the inductor: $$I(t) = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}, \ \tau = L/R$$. Inductor voltage opposes sudden change, so current cannot jump.

nodes.label: LC Oscillations
nodes.note: An $L$-$C$ loop oscillates like a spring-mass system: $$\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{q}{LC} = 0, \ \omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$$. Energy swaps between $\frac{1}{2}LI^2$ and $\frac{q^2}{2C}$.

nodes.label: Time Constant Significance
nodes.note: At $t=\tau$ growth reaches $63\%$ of final value and decay falls to $37\%$. Graph questions often ask slope at $t=0$: $dI/dt = V/L$. At $t = \tau$ the current reaches $1 - e^{-1} \approx 63\%$ of its final value.

nodes.label: Problem Archetypes and Traps
nodes.note: High-yield traps combine flux rule, energy conservation, and circuit feedback in one picture. Net charge is $$Q = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi_B)}{R}$$.

nodes.label: Ring Falling Through Field Gradient
nodes.note: A ring falling through a non-uniform field gets EMF from changing flux at top and bottom edges. Current $I = \varepsilon/R$ and magnetic drag $F = BIl$ oppose gravity. Drag force scale: $$F = \frac{B^2l^2v}{R}$$.

nodes.label: Charge in Loop Rotation
nodes.note: Rotating a loop by $90^\circ$ reverses flux sign, giving total charge flown $$Q = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{R} = \frac{2NBA}{R}$$ independent of rotation time.

nodes.label: Multi-Loop Mutual Inductance
nodes.note: Nested coils share flux through common area $A$: $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$ style scaling. Use $M_{12}=M_{21}$ to pick the easier current to differentiate. Mutual inductance scales as $$M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A l$$.

nodes.label: Flux Linkage
nodes.group: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's Laws and Lenz's Principle
nodes.note: Total flux through $N$ series turns is the flux linkage $$N\Phi_B = NAB\cos\theta$$. EMF depends on the rate of change of this quantity, which is why adding turns boosts induced voltage.

nodes.label: Motional EMF in a Moving Frame
nodes.note: In the conductor's rest frame the magnetic force on charges becomes an electric field $$\vec{E}' = \vec{v} \times \vec{B}$$. This frame view explains why motion alone can drive current.

nodes.label: Direction from Lenz's Law
nodes.note: The induced field circulates so that its own flux opposes the change: if $B$ into the page grows, induced current makes field out of the page. Fleming's right-hand rule gives the same sense. Use $$\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$ as the starting point.

nodes.label: Power Balance on the Rod
nodes.note: Mechanical power input balances Joule heating: $$F_{ext}v = I^2 R = \frac{(Blv)^2}{R}$$. Energy conservation holds at every instant of the motion.

nodes.label: Energy Needed to Build Current
nodes.note: Ramping current from $0$ to $I$ stores $$U = \int_0^I L I'\,dI' = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$$ in the inductor. This is the magnetic analogue of a capacitor's $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$.

nodes.label: Back EMF in Motors
nodes.note: A spinning coil in a motor generates back EMF $$\varepsilon_{back} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$$ opposing the supply. Net current $(V - \varepsilon_{back})/R$ sets the torque and speed balance.

nodes.label: Flux Jump Trap
nodes.note: When a loop's area or orientation snaps between two states, only the flux difference matters: $$Q = N|\Delta\Phi_B|/R$$. The time taken is irrelevant, which surprises many students.

nodes.label: Solenoid Self-Inductance
nodes.note: For a long solenoid of $n$ turns per metre and volume $V$: $$L = \mu_0 n^2 V$$. Doubling the turn density quadruples the inductance.
